                                        GUI grounding, which translates natural language instruc-               GUI grounding models are built upon Large Vision
                                        tions into precise pixel coordinates, is essential for devel-       Language Models (LVLMs), typically formulating GUI
                                        oping practical GUI agents. However, we observe that ex-            grounding as a generation task, where models output pixel
                                        isting grounding models exhibit significant coordinate pre-         coordinates as text tokens (e.g., “x=123, y=456”) [6, 10,
                                        diction instability—minor visual perturbations (e.g., crop-         24]. However, it is inherently challenging for language
                                        ping a few pixels) can drastically alter predictions, flip-         models to establish a robust correspondence between vi-
                                        ping results between correct and incorrect. This instabil-          sual elements and text coordinates tokens based on instruc-
                                        ity severely undermines model performance, especially for           tions [32, 34, 50]. Despite extensive training on GUI im-
                                        samples with high-resolution and small UI elements. To ad-          ages through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or reinforcement
                                        dress this issue, we propose Multi-View Prediction (MVP),           learning (RL), grounding models still generate unexplain-
                                        a training-free framework that enhances grounding perfor-           able erroneous coordinates, particularly when facing high-
                                        mance through multi-view inference. Our key insight is              resolution images and small target UI elements that are dif-
                                        that while single-view predictions may be unstable, aggre-          ficult to identify.
                                        gating predictions from multiple carefully cropped views                We carefully analyze the failure cases and discover that
                                        can effectively distinguish correct coordinates from out-           an incorrect prediction does not mean the model lacks the
                                        liers. MVP comprises two components: (1) Attention-                 capability to locate the target. Rather, the models suffer
                                        Guided View Proposal, which derives diverse views guided            from prediction instability, where minimal perturbations
                                        by instruction-to-image attention scores, and (2) Multi-            to input images (e.g., shifting by a few pixels) cause dra-

Figure 1. (a) An example of model’s prediction instability from ScreenSpot-Pro. The instruction is “save image in a specific format”.
Slightly shifting the screenshot causes significantly different predicted coordinates. (b) We crop different views from the original screen-
shots in ScreenSpot-Pro and then perform inference separately on them using GTA1-7B. The pass@N accuracy improves with number of
views increasing, indicting the model possessing the ability to predict the correct prediction. (c) Our MVP significantly improves perfor-
mance of different architectures and sizes grounding models by aggregating results of different views.

    (a) Prediction flips under visual perturbation.   (b) Instability intensifies with image resolution.   (c) Instability intensifies with smaller targets.

Figure 2. We evaluate model instability by adding a 28-pixel border to ScreenSpot-Pro images and performing separate inference runs with
GTA1-7B. (a) This minor visual perturbation causes 7.3% of originally correct predictions to become incorrect, and 7.8% of originally
wrong predictions to become correct, revealing high sensitivity to input variations. (b) When analyzing the distance between the two
predicted coordinates grouped by image resolution, we observe that instability increases significantly with higher resolutions. (c) Similarly,
when grouping by the area of the target region, we find that instability is more pronounced for smaller UI elements.

Figure 3. Overview of our Multiple View Prediction (MVP) pipeline, which consists of two main stages: Attention-Guided View Proposal
and Multi-Coordinate Clustering. First, MVP takes the user instruction and screenshot, forwarding through the language model to derive
attention scores from the instruction to each visual token. Then the top-k scores tokens are selected, and an h×w sub-region is cropped
around the center of each corresponding visual patch. These sub-regions are ranked by the number of top-k tokens they contain. The top-m
regions are chosen and enlarged to form the final set of views. The model independently predicts coordinates for each view. Finally, MVP
aggregates all the predictions by clustering the coordinates based on spatial proximity and outputs the center of the largest cluster as the
final prediction.

Table 1. Evaluation results on the ScreenSpot-Pro benchmark. Baseline models are evaluated using official instructions, while other mod-
els’ results are sourced from the benchmark leaderboard. Our method shows significant performance improvements across all categories.
These consistent gains across diverse model architectures validate MVP’s effectiveness in addressing high-resolution GUI grounding chal-
lenges through its multi-view prediction mechanism.
